messages:
Mia: Hey all — first week onboarding. Trying to keep my dev env consistent between an M1 MacBook and a Windows Surface. Running into SSH/GPG/dotfiles weirdness when switching contexts. Anyone got a concise checklist?

Ravi: welcome! quick Qs: are you using WSL or native Windows for dev? which dotfiles manager (stow/chezmoi/bare git)? asdf for runtimes?

Mia: thx. Using WSL2 for shells and most builds, but I occasionally use Windows side apps (VSCode native) and the Git GUI. Dotfiles are a bare git + stow symlink setup. asdf for node/python/ruby. Problems: SSH agent not forwarding into WSL/VSCode, GPG commit signing failing on Windows git, direnv sometimes refuses to load .envrc when I switch OS.

Sam: short advice: pick one runtime as authoritative (I pick WSL for windows laptop). Avoid NTFS symlinks from Windows side — permissions and symlink types bite you. Chezmoi handles per-OS templating really nicely if you want single repo with platform blocks.

Alex: SSH/GPG split is common. If you keep keys in 1Password, run the 1Password CLI inside the same OS/runtime your editor/git uses. On mac I run `eval $(op agent --enable)` in my shell. On WSL install the linux op binary and `op signin` in WSL so the agent socket is available there.

Ravi: For SSH agent bridging from Windows to WSL a pragmatic approach: enable and start the Windows ssh-agent service (`Start-Service ssh-agent`) and add your key (`ssh-add C:\Users\YOU\.ssh\id_ed25519`). From WSL, point SSH_AUTH_SOCK to the Windows agent socket path. There are multiple ways; VSCode + Remote-WSL with agent forwarding is easiest: set `remote.SSH.enableAgentForwarding` to true in your VSCode user settings.

Mia: I tried using the Windows op app and expected WSL to see it — that failed. Also direnv kept flagging my .envrc as changed even when I hadn't edited it.

Sam: direnv shoutout: check CRLFs. If your repo checked out files with CRLF on Windows, direnv signature differs. Run `dos2unix .envrc` or configure git core.autocrlf properly. Also ensure you ran `direnv allow` after fixes and that your shell has the direnv hook (e.g., `eval "$(direnv hook bash)"`).

Alex: GPG signing error often means Git is invoking gpg in a different environment than your keys. If VSCode is using Windows Git while your keys live in WSL gpg, signing fails with `gpg: signing failed: No pinentry`. Fix by either using Remote-WSL so VSCode runs the git you expect, or configure VSCode git to the WSL git executable. Also confirm `git config --global user.signingkey <KEYID>` and that `GPG_TTY` is set: `export GPG_TTY=$(tty)` in your shell.

Mia: OK — plan I'm going to try: 1) pick WSL as authoritative runtime, 2) install op inside WSL and `op signin`, 3) run `dos2unix .envrc` and `direnv allow`, 4) move to Remote-WSL in VSCode so Git/gpg/ssh are consistent, 5) run `asdf reshim` and ensure `source ~/.asdf/asdf.sh` in both shells. Anything else?

Ravi: that's solid. extra tips: for Homebrew on M1 ensure `/opt/homebrew/bin` is before `/usr/local` in PATH; for asdf add language build deps in WSL (`sudo apt install -y libssl-dev zlib1g-dev build-essential`). If you keep some Windows-native tools, enable Developer Mode to ease symlink creation if you ever need them.

Sam: I also recommend adding a small README in your dotfiles repo with OS-specific steps (like 'if on Windows, run these WSL steps', 'if mac do Brew path tweak'). Saves time for future reboots.

Mia: super helpful, thanks everyone. I'll make the changes and report back. If anyone wants to pair tomorrow around 10:30am PT to confirm VSCode remote flows, ping me.

Ravi: pinged you — devex office hours tomorrow 11am too if you want quick live help :thumbsup:

Mia: awesome, appreciate it :rocket:
